error_modes.label: Lateral separation in fingertip on the route legs

texts.0: SP, due to lateral inputs applied only after the sight picture had completely changed, did not preserve the 10 ft minimum lateral separation reference while flying fingertip on the navigation legs. Spacing opened past 30 ft in the turns at the turning points and on one roll out closed inside the 10 ft reference, which the criteria do not permit in either direction. IP intervened on the controls to re-establish a safe lateral distance before the next leg was flown.
texts.1: SP, due to aileron and rudder corrections started only after the leader had already rolled out, allowed lateral separation to reach about 28 to 30 ft on the outbound legs, at the outer edge of the tolerance. The spacing was brought back toward the reference only after repeated verbal prompts from IP. No control intervention was needed, but no correction was initiated by SP without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a lateral correction begun after the widening had already developed, let separation grow to roughly 20 to 25 ft in the turns onto the second and third legs. SP recognized the wider sight picture, applied a small coordinated input toward the leader and re-established the reference within a few seconds. No prompting and no intervention by IP were required.
texts.3: SP held lateral separation inside the plus 10 ft tolerance for the whole formation portion of the navigation, working between 10 and 20 ft from the reference through the level legs, the en route climb and the turns at the turning points. Corrections were small, early and made with coordinated aileron and rudder. The 10 ft minimum was never eroded on either side of the leader.
texts.4: SP flew lateral separation within a couple of feet of the 10 ft reference for the entire route, including every turning point and the en route descent. Lateral inputs were made as the leader's bank developed rather than after the picture had changed. The spacing appeared visually constant from the rear cockpit throughout the formation legs.
texts.marginal: SP kept lateral separation within standards, but worked continuously near the plus 10 ft edge, most consistently on the right side and in the second half of each turn. The tendency was toward widening rather than closing, so no safety margin was lost, but the position flown was not the briefed one. SP is expected to bring the working band back toward the reference line on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew fingertip lateral separation with IP calling the correction needed to hold the 10 ft minimum reference, due to this being one of the first fingertip legs SP has flown holding lateral separation against a stated minimum reference rather than a general picture. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to hold more of the lateral reference independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP preserved the 10 ft minimum lateral separation reference while flying fingertip, holding the working spacing to about 18 ft, at the edge of the standard, due to the aileron correction being started only after the sight picture had already opened rather than as it began to open. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to start the aileron correction as the sight picture begins to open, not after.
texts_at.2: SP preserved the 10 ft minimum lateral separation reference while flying fingertip, holding the working spacing to about 15 ft, due to the correction being applied a beat after the leader rolled out rather than with the roll-out. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply the correction with the leader's roll-out, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP preserved the 10 ft minimum lateral separation reference while flying fingertip, holding the working spacing to about 8 ft over the reference, due to the coordinated input being sized a fraction less than the widening required before it was refined. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to size the coordinated input to the widening on the first attempt.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good lateral-separation discipline.

The only refinement available was to hold that same precision through the sharpest turn of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good lateral-separation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew lateral separation within a couple of feet of the minimum lateral reference for the entire route, including every turning point and the en route descent, lateral inputs made as the leader's bank developed rather than after the picture had changed with the spacing appearing visually constant from the rear cockpit. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent lateral-separation discipline.

error_modes.label: Vertical separation and stack position as wingman

texts.0: SP, due to power corrections made without a matching pitch reference on the leader's canopy line, did not maintain the fingertip stack and allowed vertical separation to wander throughout the formation legs. Deviations exceeded 10 ft low during the en route climb and reached more than 6 ft high after the second turning point, outside the limits in both directions. IP intervened on the controls to restore the stack when SP settled low and behind the leader's wing line.
texts.1: SP, due to a vertical reference taken from the leader's wing tip instead of the briefed canopy line, held the stack about 9 to 10 ft low through the second leg, at the limit of the tolerance. The position was raised only after IP called the deviation twice. The correction was late but was completed without any control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch input delayed after the leader's power reduction, let vertical separation reach about 6 to 8 ft low during the en route descent. SP identified the change in the sight picture, added a small amount of back pressure together with power and returned the stack toward the reference before the next turning point. No prompting or intervention by IP was needed.
texts.3: SP held vertical separation within plus or minus 4 ft of the briefed stack for the whole formation portion of the route. The level legs, the en route climb and the descent were all flown with the leader's reference line in the same place on the canopy. Pitch and power inputs were small and were made as the leader's attitude changed.
texts.4: SP kept the stack essentially fixed, with vertical deviations of a foot or two through the entire route including the turns at each turning point. The reference line on the leader's aircraft stayed in the same position on the canopy in level flight, in the climb and in the descent. Vertical deviations were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside the plus or minus 4 ft tolerance, but flew consistently on the low side of the stack and recovered the reference only slowly after each power change. The trend is toward a position that becomes progressively lower as the leader changes speed and altitude on the later legs. SP is expected to fly the briefed reference line rather than a habitual low stack on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the fingertip stack with IP calling the pitch reference on the leader's canopy line needed to hold vertical separation, due to this being one of the first fingertip legs SP has flown holding the stack to a specific canopy reference. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to hold more of the canopy reference independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the fingertip stack with vertical separation to about 9 ft low, at the edge of the standard, due to the pitch reference being taken from the leader's wing tip rather than the briefed canopy line. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to take the pitch reference from the briefed canopy line, not the wing tip.
texts_at.2: SP held the fingertip stack with vertical separation to about 7 ft low, due to the back pressure following the leader's power reduction by a beat rather than matching it directly. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to match the back pressure directly to the leader's power change, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP held the fingertip stack with vertical separation to about 4 ft low, due to the stack being returned toward the reference a fraction after the sight picture changed rather than as it changed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to return the stack toward the reference as the sight picture changes, not a fraction after.

error_modes.label: Observance angle and fore-aft geometry as wingman

texts.0: SP, due to power handling that lagged the leader's speed changes on the route, did not hold the nominal observance angle and lost the fore-aft geometry of the fingertip position. SP fell aft beyond 60 deg approaching the second turning point and then closed with excess overtake toward line abreast, well outside the permitted band. IP intervened on the throttle and the controls to re-establish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to throttle movement applied only after the leader had already accelerated on the outbound leg, allowed the observance angle to open to about 50 deg, at the limit of the tolerance. The geometry was recovered toward the reference only after IP called the aft drift and directed the power increase. The angle remained near the outer limit for most of that leg.
texts.2: SP, due to a small power reduction held slightly too long after the turn onto the third leg, let the observance angle open to roughly 40 deg. SP recognized the aft movement in the sight picture, added power in a single measured step and returned to the reference geometry without generating overtake. No verbal prompting or IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained the 30 deg observance angle within plus or minus 5 deg for the formation portion of the route. The fore-aft geometry was held through the en route climb, the level legs and the turns at each turning point, with power used in small anticipatory steps. Overtake was contained at all times and the position was never allowed to slide aft.
texts.4: SP held the observance angle within a degree or two of 30 deg for the whole route, with no visible fore-aft movement even during the leader's speed changes at the turning points. Power was set ahead of the leader's changes rather than in response to them. Geometry deviations were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the observance angle inside the plus or minus 5 deg tolerance, but flew habitually toward the aft edge of the band and recovered slowly whenever the leader accelerated. The trend is toward a position that will move outside tolerance as soon as the speed changes on the route become larger. SP is expected to anticipate the power requirement and fly the nominal 30 deg reference on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the fore-aft geometry with IP calling the throttle movement needed to hold the nominal observance angle, due to this being one of the first fingertip legs SP has flown holding the observance angle against the leader's speed changes. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to time more of the throttle movement independently with the leader's speed changes on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP held the fore-aft geometry with the observance angle to about 52 deg, at the edge of the standard, due to the throttle movement being applied only after the leader had already accelerated rather than with the acceleration. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply the throttle movement with the leader's acceleration, not after it.
texts_at.2: SP held the fore-aft geometry with the observance angle to about 40 deg, due to the power reduction being held a beat longer than the turn required before it was eased. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to ease the power reduction as soon as the turn no longer requires it.
texts_at.3: SP held the fore-aft geometry with the observance angle to about 32 deg, due to the measured power step being applied a fraction after the aft movement was noticed rather than in the same motion. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply the power step in the same motion the aft movement is noticed.

texts_above.3: SP maintained the 30 deg observance angle to about 32 deg through the formation portion of the route, overtake contained at all times with the position never allowed to slide aft. The only refinement available was to hold that same anticipation through the leader's fastest speed change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to well-developed fore-aft-geometry discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the observance angle within a degree or two of 30 deg for the whole route, with no visible fore-aft movement even during the leader's speed changes at the turning points, power set ahead of the leader's changes rather than in response to them with geometry deviations negligible. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding fore-aft-geometry discipline.

error_modes.label: Control smoothness, power handling and trim as wingman

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs made in large discrete steps rather than as continuous pressures, did not control the aircraft in a smooth and solid way and used abrupt corrections throughout the formation legs. Power was swung between very low and very high settings and the aircraft was left out of trim for the whole en route climb, so each correction produced a further deviation. IP had to take control to stabilize the aircraft in position.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check locked onto a single point on the leader, flew the position with a series of abrupt corrections and did not trim the aircraft after the en route climb. The technique improved only after IP described the required continuous control pressures and prompted for trim on two occasions. The aircraft stayed in position, but the corrections were still coarse at the end of the leg.
texts.2: SP, due to control pressures released too early after each correction, produced several noticeable step inputs on the first formation leg. SP recognized the pattern, moved to continuous small pressures and trimmed the aircraft before the turning point, after which the corrections were smooth. No prompting or intervention by IP was needed.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way, without abrupt corrections, during the whole formation portion of the navigation. Engine power was used properly in small anticipatory changes and the aircraft was trimmed continuously through the climb, the level legs and the descent. Position corrections were made with pressures rather than with displacements.
texts.4: SP flew the fingertip position with continuous, almost imperceptible control pressures for the entire route. Power and trim were adjusted ahead of every change of speed and altitude, so no recovery input was ever required. The handling technique was well above the level expected at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP flew within standards, but the corrections were still made as small discrete inputs rather than as continuous pressures, and the aircraft was retrimmed late after each change of speed. The trend is toward rising workload and fatigue on longer formation legs, which will show up as larger deviations later in the sortie. SP is expected to fly the position on pressures and to trim continuously on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the fingertip position with IP calling when to trim and demonstrating the continuous pressures needed to stay smooth, due to this being one of the first formation legs SP has flown controlling the aircraft with continuous pressures rather than discrete corrections. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to hold more of the continuous pressures independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way during the formation legs, due to one correction being made as a discrete step before it was smoothed into a continuous pressure. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to make every correction a continuous pressure from the first input, not a discrete step.
texts_at.2: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way during the formation legs, due to the trim being reset a beat after a speed change rather than continuously through it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to trim continuously through every speed change, not a beat after.
texts_at.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way during the formation legs, due to one control pressure being released a fraction early before the correction was fully in. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold every control pressure through to the full correction, not release it early.

texts_above.1: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way during the formation legs. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way, without abrupt corrections, during the whole formation portion of the navigation, engine power used in small anticipatory changes and the aircraft trimmed continuously through the climb, the level legs and the descent. Holding every control pressure through to the full correction, rather than releasing it early, would smooth the technique further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady control-smoothness discipline.
texts_above.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid way with position corrections made with pressures rather than displacements, the technique free of any abrupt step through the whole formation portion of the route. The only refinement available was to hold that same smoothness through the longest formation leg of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate control-smoothness discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the fingertip position with continuous, almost imperceptible control pressures for the entire route, power and trim adjusted ahead of every change of speed and altitude so no recovery input was ever required, the handling technique well above the level expected at this stage of training. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary control-smoothness discipline.

error_modes.label: Speed brake use and overtake control from both sides

texts.0: SP, due to overtake being recognized only at close range, did not use the speed brake when required and was left with no effective means of controlling closure on the leader. Closure continued from the aft position until the aircraft was inside the briefed geometry on the right side, and the speed brake was extended only on the IP's command. IP intervened on the controls to open the position and restore separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a power reduction judged sufficient without the speed brake, allowed overtake to develop until the position could only be held by a large lateral displacement. The speed brake was extended after IP directed it, and only from the left side; the same correction was not made when in the right position. Closure was contained without control intervention, but not on SP's own initiative.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction made late after the leader decelerated at the turning point, developed a noticeable overtake on the outside of the turn. SP extended the speed brake without prompting, retracted it once the closure had stopped and re-established the position from the right side with no further correction. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP used the speed brake correctly following the leader's command and whenever it was needed to keep overtake under control, from both the left and the right side. Extension and retraction were timed so that closure was stopped without opening the position. Power and speed brake were used together rather than one after the other.
texts.4: SP anticipated every closure situation on the route and used short, small speed brake extensions before overtake became visible, working equally well from both sides. Each extension was matched with a power change so that the position never moved more than a few feet from the reference. The control of overtake was well above the level expected at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP kept overtake under control within standards, but used the speed brake almost exclusively from the left side and reverted to power alone when flying in the right position. The trend is toward a technique that will not contain closure during the larger speed changes required on later navigation profiles. SP is expected to practise speed brake use from both sides on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP used the speed brake with IP calling when to extend and retract it from each side, due to this being one of the first formation legs SP has flown using the speed brake to control overtake from both sides. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to judge more of the speed brake timing independently from both sides on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP used the speed brake correctly whenever needed to keep overtake under control, due to the extension from the right side being judged a beat later than the same extension would be from the left. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to judge the speed brake extension the same way from either side, not later from the right.
texts_at.2: SP used the speed brake correctly whenever needed to keep overtake under control, due to the retraction following the closure stopping by a fraction rather than at the same instant. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to retract the speed brake at the instant closure stops, not a fraction after.
texts_at.3: SP used the speed brake correctly whenever needed to keep overtake under control, due to power and speed brake being used a beat apart on one occasion rather than together. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to use power and speed brake together, not a beat apart.

texts_above.1: SP used the speed brake correctly whenever needed to keep overtake under control. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP used the speed brake correctly following the leader's command and whenever needed to keep overtake under control, from both the left and the right side, extension and retraction timed so closure was stopped without opening the position. Using power and speed brake together, rather than a beat apart, would tighten the closure control further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable speed-brake discipline.
texts_above.3: SP used the speed brake correctly from both sides with power and speed brake used together rather than one after the other, closure contained on every occasion it was needed through the route. The only refinement available was to hold that same two-sided technique through the largest speed change of the route. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good speed-brake discipline.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated every closure situation on the route and used short, small speed brake extensions before overtake became visible, working equally well from both sides, each extension matched with a power change so the position never moved more than a few feet from the reference with control of overtake well above the level expected at this stage of training. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior speed-brake discipline.

error_modes.label: Preservation of the briefed fingertip position through turning points and side changes

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that left the change of side and the turning point work to be done at the same moment, did not preserve the fingertip position determined in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The position was flown from a self-selected reference instead of the briefed one, and after the crossunder SP stabilized where none of the specified separations or the observance angle were met. IP intervened to place the aircraft back in the briefed position before the next leg.
texts.1: SP, due to a workload plan that treated route timing and position keeping as tasks to be done one after the other, did not re-establish the briefed sight picture after the change to the left side and held a position visibly wide and aft of it. The correct references were adopted again only after IP described the required picture. The position was then held at the outer edge of the stated deviations for the rest of the leg.
texts.2: SP, due to attention given to the turning point timing during the change of side, initially stabilized outside the briefed picture after the crossunder. SP compared the actual sight picture with the briefed references, corrected in one step and settled inside the specified deviations before the leg was established. No prompting or intervention by IP was needed.
texts.3: SP preserved the fingertip position determined in the Techniques and Procedures Manual throughout the formation portion of the navigation, within the deviations stated in the specific criteria. The briefed references were used on both sides of the leader and were re-established immediately after each change of side. Route duties and position keeping were carried out without either task degrading the other.
texts.4: SP held the briefed fingertip position on both sides of the leader with no perceptible change of picture across the turning points, the changes of side and the en route climb and descent. All route duties were completed without the aircraft moving out of position at any stage. Deviations from the briefed references were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP held the briefed position within the stated deviations, but the picture was re-established noticeably more slowly after each change of side and drifted while the route timing was being checked. The trend is toward position keeping that degrades whenever a second task is added, which will not be sustainable on longer formation legs. SP is expected to fly the briefed references continuously while completing route duties on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP held the fingertip position through the turning points with IP calling the briefed references to re-establish after each change of side, due to this being one of the first formation legs SP has flown re-establishing the briefed picture after a change of side. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to re-establish more of the briefed picture independently after a change of side on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP preserved the fingertip position determined in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, due to the sight picture after a change of side being re-established a beat after the crossunder rather than through it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to re-establish the sight picture through the crossunder itself, not a beat after.
texts_at.2: SP preserved the fingertip position determined in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, due to the position drifting a fraction while route timing was checked before it was corrected. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the position steady while route timing is checked, not let it drift.
texts_at.3: SP preserved the fingertip position determined in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, due to the briefed references being compared against the actual picture a moment after the change of side rather than during it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to compare the briefed references against the actual picture during the change of side, not a moment after.

Comparing the briefed references against the actual picture during the change of side, rather than a moment after, would tighten the recovery further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to assured position-preservation discipline.

Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate position-preservation discipline.

error_modes.label: Division of attention between formation position and navigation and lookout duties

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck in which the fingertip sight picture absorbed the entire scan, did not carry out any navigation or lookout duty during the formation legs. Turning points were overflown, route timing was not maintained and no clearing was performed for the formation while the position was being flown. IP had to take over the navigation and then direct SP back onto the route.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the leader to the exclusion of everything else, did not check the route timing or clear the formation until IP called for each item in turn. The navigation tasks were completed only after prompting and one turning point was reached about a minute late. Position keeping itself stayed inside the deviations, but no capacity was left for anything else.
texts.2: SP, due to the scan narrowing onto the leader after the first turning point, initially fell behind the route timing and stopped clearing outside the formation. SP recognized the omission, re-established the alternation between position keeping and the route and lookout tasks, and reached the next turning point on time. No prompting or intervention by IP was required.
texts.3: SP divided attention between the fingertip position and the navigation and lookout duties throughout the formation legs. Turning points, timing and clearing were completed while the position was held inside the specified deviations. Neither the position nor the route work degraded while the other task was in progress.
texts.4: SP kept the route running, the timing accurate and the lookout continuous while holding a fingertip position that did not visibly move. Fuel checks and turning point calls were made on schedule with no interruption to position keeping. The division of attention was well above the level expected at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP kept both the position and the route work within standards, but the navigation tasks were compressed into short bursts and each one was followed by a small excursion in position. The trend is toward a scan that can serve only one task at a time, which will show as missed timing or lost position on a longer or busier route. SP is expected to alternate attention more evenly on the next sortie.

texts_at.0: SP divided attention between the fingertip position and the route with IP calling when to check timing and when to return to the position, due to this being one of the first formation navigation legs SP has flown dividing attention between position and route duties. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to divide more of the attention independently between position and route duties on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP divided attention between the fingertip position and the navigation and lookout duties, due to one navigation task being compressed into a burst that produced a small excursion in position afterward. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to spread every navigation task evenly rather than compress it into a burst.
texts_at.2: SP divided attention between the fingertip position and the navigation and lookout duties, due to the alternation between position and route work leaning a beat toward the route task before it returned to position. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to keep the alternation even between position and route work, not lean toward one.
texts_at.3: SP divided attention between the fingertip position and the navigation and lookout duties, due to one small excursion in position being recovered a fraction after the navigation task ended rather than as it ended. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to recover any small excursion as the navigation task ends, not a fraction after.

error_modes.label: Leading the formation on the route with regard to the wingman

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of the wingman's position with regard to the sun and the route boundaries, did not execute the planned maneuvers smoothly as leader and did not maintain positive pressure on the flying controls. The turns at the turning points were entered with abrupt bank changes that placed No2 into the sun twice, and one turn was started too late for the airspace boundary. IP took control to reposition the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to attention limited to own navigation while leading, entered the turns at the turning points with roll rates the wingman could not comfortably follow and gave no consideration to where No2 would end up relative to the sun. The maneuvers were flown more smoothly and the direction of turn was changed only after IP described the effect on the wingman. Nothing beyond verbal direction was required, but no allowance was made by SP alone.
texts.2: SP, due to a first turn initiated at a roll rate higher than briefed, made position keeping difficult for No2 on the second leg. SP noticed the size of the wingman's corrections, reduced the roll rate, maintained positive pressure on the flying controls through the remaining maneuvers and planned the following turns away from the sun. No IP prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP led the navigation smoothly, executing and completing each planned maneuver with steady bank and pitch rates and maintaining positive pressure on the flying controls. The wingman's position with regard to the sun and the route and area boundaries was taken into consideration when each turn was planned. No2 was able to hold the fingertip position throughout without large corrections.
texts.4: SP led the route with maneuver entries so smooth and so well planned that No2 held position with no visible correction. Every turn was set up to keep the wingman clear of the sun and inside the route and area boundaries, and control pressures stayed positive through the whole profile. The standard of leadership was well above the level expected at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP led within standards, but the roll rates at the turning points were at the upper end of what No2 could follow and the sun position was considered only after the turn had been started. The trend is toward maneuvering that will push the wingman outside tolerance as soon as bank angles increase. SP is expected to plan the turns around the wingman's position and to hold steadier control pressures on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Correcting one reference at a time in the order stack, fore-aft, lateral

texts.0: SP, due to attempting to correct more than one reference at a time instead of setting the vertical stack first, did not rebuild the fingertip position at any point of the formation legs. Pitch, power and bank corrections were applied together, so the stack ran past 10 ft low, the observance angle swept beyond the aft limit and the spacing closed inside the 10 ft lateral reference during the same turning point. IP took the controls to re-establish the position before the next leg.
texts.1: SP, due to working the lateral spacing and the stack simultaneously rather than in the sequence vertical, fore-aft, lateral, drove the deviations to the outer limits at about 6 ft high and near 30 ft of spacing on the outbound legs. The correction order was applied only after IP called for the stack to be set first and the spacing to be left alone. No control intervention was needed, but the sequence was never adopted unprompted.
texts.2: SP, due to a combined pitch and bank correction attempted at the first turning point, let the stack run about 6 ft low while the spacing opened to roughly 20 to 25 ft. SP recognized that the two corrections were interfering with each other, set the vertical position first, then the fore-aft reference and last the lateral spacing. The sequence was restored without prompting or IP intervention.
texts.3: SP corrected one reference at a time in the order given in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, setting the vertical stack first, then the fore-aft reference line and finally the lateral spacing in or out. No single deviation exceeded 4 ft vertically or 20 ft laterally while another reference was being worked. The fingertip picture was rebuilt after every turning point with no residual error left in any axis.
texts.4: SP isolated each deviation and cleared it in the briefed order before addressing the next, so that no more than one or two feet of vertical error and a couple of feet of lateral error ever accumulated on the route. Because only one reference was in work at any moment, the corrections did not interact and the sight picture stayed visually constant through the climb, the level legs and each turning point.
texts.marginal: SP used the correct correction order, but on several legs started the lateral adjustment before the stack had fully settled, so two references were momentarily worked together. The deviations stayed inside the tolerances and the picture was always recovered before the next turning point. SP is expected to complete the vertical correction before beginning the lateral one on the next navigation sortie.

error_modes.label: Over correction of power and the three PCL movements of a power correction

texts.0: SP, due to over correction of power with whole arm PCL movements instead of the three small movements that start, stop and stabilize the aircraft, did not control the fore-aft position at any stage of the formation legs. Each power change produced a larger deviation in the opposite direction, so the observance angle oscillated well beyond the aft limit and then closed toward line abreast with uncontrolled overtake. IP intervened on the throttle to stop the divergence.
texts.1: SP, due to power corrections made with a single large PCL movement and no movement to stop the aircraft, allowed the observance angle to reach about 50 deg aft and then to overshoot forward on every recovery. The oscillation was damped only after IP called for smaller power changes and for the stopping movement to be added. No control intervention was required, but no correction was completed by SP without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a power increase left in too long without the second PCL movement to stop the aircraft, generated a noticeable forward overshoot after the first turning point, with the observance angle running to roughly 40 deg and back. SP recognized the over correction, changed to small wrist movements of the PCL and completed the following corrections with a movement to start, one to stop and one to stabilize. No prompting or IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP made power corrections with three PCL movements throughout the formation portion of the route, one to start the correction, one to stop the aircraft and one to stabilize it in the desired position. The observance angle was held within plus or minus 5 deg of 30 deg and no overshoot developed after any power change. PCL inputs were made with the wrist rather than the whole arm.
texts.4: SP applied power in small wrist movements that were so well judged that the stopping and stabilizing movements were barely perceptible from the rear cockpit. The fore-aft position was regained after each of the leader's speed changes with no overshoot at all and deviations of no more than a degree or two of observance angle. Power discipline was above the level expected at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP kept the fore-aft position inside the tolerances, but consistently used one large PCL movement followed by a late correcting movement, so each power change was followed by a small overshoot. No deviation exceeded the limits and every overshoot was contained. SP is expected to break each power correction into the three small movements on the next navigation sortie.

The position stabilized with the stack outside the 6 ft high to 10 ft low band and the observance angle beyond the aft limit on both sides of the leader. IP intervened to rebuild the position from the correct references.
texts.1: SP, due to a vertical reference taken from the leader's canopy rather than from the exhaust stack on top of the closest wing, settled about 6 ft high with the fore-aft picture at the aft limit for most of the first two legs. texts.2: SP, due to the fore-aft reference being read from the wing leading edge instead of the aft wingtip light on the front edge of the exhaust stack opening, stabilized around 40 deg of observance angle after the first turning point. texts.3: SP flew the fingertip position from the briefed front cockpit references throughout the formation legs, keeping the exhaust stack on top of the leader's closest wing, the aft wingtip light on the front edge of the exhaust stack opening and the front cockpit pilot aligned with the forward edge of the leader's horizontal stabilizer. The resulting position stayed within 4 ft vertically and within 30 deg plus or minus 5 deg of observance angle. The same references were used on both sides of the leader.
texts.4: SP used the briefed references so consistently that the sight picture was reproduced identically after every turning point and after each change of side, with vertical error of a foot or two and no visible fore-aft movement. Corrections were referred back to the manual references rather than to a remembered picture. Reference discipline was above the level expected at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP used the briefed references, but tended to read the vertical position from the leader's wing as a whole rather than from the exhaust stack on the closest wing, so the stack was habitually flown toward the high edge of the band. Tolerances were not exceeded and the position was always recoverable. SP is expected to check the position against each of the three briefed references in turn on the next navigation sortie.

texts.3: SP avoided any tendency to focus or stare at a single reference and read the fingertip picture as a whole through the climb, the level legs and each turning point. texts.4: SP kept the scan moving continuously across the vertical, fore-aft and lateral references, so every deviation was recognized while it was still no more than a foot or two. On one turn SP began a roll out and then suddenly rolled back into the bank, which drove the wingman past the lateral and vertical limits at the same time. IP took control to steady the formation.

No control intervention was needed, but no turn was flown smoothly without prompting.
texts.2: SP, as leader, due to a ratcheted roll into the turn onto the second leg, made the wingman work through a spacing excursion of roughly 20 to 25 ft. SP recognized the effect on the wingman, stopped the roll, paused momentarily to allow the wingman to adjust and then rolled smoothly back into the turn. The remaining turning points were flown at consistent roll rates without prompting.
texts.3: SP, as leader, entered and exited every turn at the turning points with a consistent, predictable roll rate and did not stair-step or ratchet the roll or reverse the bank once a roll out had been started. The wingman held the fingertip position within the specified deviations throughout each turn. Where a turn had to be continued for route orientation, the roll was stopped, a short pause was allowed and the turn was resumed smoothly.
texts.4: SP, as leader, produced roll rates so consistent that the wingman's corrections were not visible at any turning point, and every roll out was completed without any tendency to roll back into the bank. Pitch, bank and G were blended smoothly through all the route turns. The platform provided was above the standard expected at this stage of training.

The only refinement available was to hold that same consistency through the tightest turn of the route. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise roll-rate-continuity discipline.
texts_above.4: SP, as leader, produced roll rates so consistent that the wingman's corrections were not visible at any turning point, every roll out completed without any tendency to roll back into the bank, pitch, bank and G blended smoothly through all the route turns with the platform provided above the standard expected at this stage of training. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate roll-rate-continuity discipline.

error_modes.label: Lag pursuit in turns away and forward pressure in turns into at the turning points

texts.0: SP, as wingman, due to failing to add back pressure and power in the lag pursuit position of the turns away from the leader, did not climb with the leader at the turning points and the stack collapsed well past 10 ft low. In the turns into the leader no forward pressure or power reduction was applied, so the aircraft moved high and forward with closure toward the leader. IP intervened on the controls to restore separation before the next leg.
texts.1: SP, as wingman, due to back pressure applied in the turns away without the accompanying power increase, arrived at the low edge of the vertical band and hung at the aft limit of the observance angle. Power was added only after IP called for it, and the power reduction at the completion of the relative climb came late enough to leave the aircraft forward. The limits were held, but every correction followed the deviation.
texts.2: SP, as wingman, due to late recognition of the lag pursuit position at the first turning point, let the stack fall about 6 ft low before increasing back pressure and adding power. SP identified the pattern, climbed with the leader at the following turning points and reduced power as the leader stopped the roll-in and the relative climb was complete. Turns into the leader were then flown with slight forward pressure and a matching power reduction without prompting.
texts.3: SP, as wingman, recognized the lag pursuit position in every turn away from the leader and increased back pressure with a matching power increase to climb and hold airspeed, reducing power as the leader stopped the roll-in. In the turns into the leader, slight forward pressure with a power reduction kept the vertical position within 4 ft and the observance angle within plus or minus 5 deg of 30 deg.
texts.4: SP, as wingman, anticipated the lag pursuit geometry from the leader's roll input, so the back pressure, the power increase and the following power reduction were applied as the turn developed rather than after any displacement appeared. Turns into the leader were flown with barely perceptible forward pressure and matching power. The stack varied by no more than a foot or two either side through every turning point.
texts.marginal: SP, as wingman, handled both turn directions inside the standards, but the power reduction at the end of the relative climb was consistently a beat late, leaving a small forward tendency at each roll out. The vertical band was never exceeded and no closure toward the leader developed. SP is expected to reduce power as the leader stops the roll-in on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP, as wingman, flew the lag pursuit turns with IP calling the back pressure and power needed in the turn away and the forward pressure needed in the turn into the leader, due to this being one of the first formation legs SP has flown correcting for lag pursuit geometry in both turn directions. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to apply more of the lag pursuit correction independently in both turn directions on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP, as wingman, recognized the lag pursuit position in every turn away from the leader, holding vertical position to about 4 ft, at the edge of the standard, due to the power reduction at the end of the relative climb following the leader's roll-in stop by a beat. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power as the leader stops the roll-in, not a beat after.
texts_at.2: SP, as wingman, recognized the lag pursuit position in every turn away from the leader, holding vertical position to about 3 ft, due to the back pressure in the turn away being matched a fraction after the leader's climb rate rather than with it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to match back pressure with the leader's climb rate, not a fraction after.
texts_at.3: SP, as wingman, recognized the lag pursuit position in every turn away from the leader, holding vertical position to about 2 ft, due to the forward pressure in the turn into the leader being applied a fraction after the roll-in rather than with it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply forward pressure with the roll-in itself, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP, as wingman, recognized the lag pursuit position in every turn away from the leader, holding vertical position to about 4 ft, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP, as wingman, recognized the lag pursuit position in every turn away from the leader and increased back pressure with a matching power increase, reducing power as the leader stopped the roll-in, vertical position held within about 7 ft with the observance angle held close to the nominal reference. Applying forward pressure with the roll-in itself, rather than a fraction after, would tighten the vertical hold further. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to competent lag-pursuit discipline.
texts_above.3: SP, as wingman, handled both turn directions with vertical position held within about 2 ft, back pressure and power increase applied as the turn developed rather than after any displacement appeared. The only refinement available was to hold that same anticipation through the leader's fastest roll-in. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined lag-pursuit discipline.
texts_above.4: SP, as wingman, anticipated the lag pursuit geometry from the leader's roll input, so the back pressure, the power increase and the following power reduction were applied as the turn developed rather than after any displacement appeared, turns into the leader flown with barely perceptible forward pressure and matching power with the stack varying by no more than a foot or two either side through every turning point. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless lag-pursuit discipline.

error_modes.label: Low and near zero G segments and uncommanded movement toward Number 1

texts.0: SP, due to a pushover to the en route descent flown at near zero G without regard to the reduced ability to counteract movement toward the leader, did not arrest the drift inboard and attempted to correct with bank alone, which produces no heading change in that condition. The aircraft closed inside the 10 ft lateral reference and no breakout was initiated. IP intervened on the controls to open the position.
texts.1: SP, due to a low G letdown entered without unloading the closure first, drifted to the inner edge of the lateral band and held there because bank alone was not producing lateral movement. The drift was arrested only after IP called for positive G to be re-established before correcting. No control intervention was required, but the recovery was not initiated by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to a light G pushover at the start of the descent leg, initially developed a small inboard drift and a single wing rock from the leader's wingtip vortices. SP recognized that bank alone would not stop the movement, re-established positive G, corrected laterally and stabilized at the reference. No prompting or IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP maintained positive G through the pushover into the en route descent and through every reduced G segment of the route, so lateral corrections remained effective at all times. Lateral separation stayed inside the 10 ft to 20 ft band and no uncommanded movement toward the leader was allowed to develop. The position was flown clear of the leader's wingtip vortices.
texts.4: SP anticipated every reduced G segment, kept the aircraft loaded enough for the flight controls to remain fully effective and stepped the position slightly clear of the leader's wingtip vortices before the pushover. No inboard drift occurred and lateral separation varied by no more than a couple of feet. Awareness of the low G limitation was above the level expected at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP kept lateral separation within standards during the low G portions of the route, but allowed the G to reduce close to zero at the start of the descent and corrected initially with bank before reloading the aircraft. No limit was exceeded and the drift was small. SP is expected to maintain positive G through pushovers and to correct with G before bank on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP flew the reduced G segment with IP calling when to reload positive G before correcting laterally, due to this being one of the first reduced G segments SP has flown keeping the G positive enough for the lateral corrections to remain effective. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to keep more of the G positive independently through reduced G segments on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP maintained positive G through the pushover into the en route descent, holding lateral separation to about 18 ft, at the edge of the standard, due to the G being allowed to reduce close to zero before it was reloaded. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to keep the G comfortably positive through the pushover, not reduce it close to zero.
texts_at.2: SP maintained positive G through the pushover into the en route descent, holding lateral separation to about 15 ft, due to the initial correction being made with bank before the G was reloaded rather than after. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to reload the G before correcting with bank, not after.
texts_at.3: SP maintained positive G through the pushover into the en route descent, holding lateral separation to about 8 ft, due to the aircraft being stepped clear of the wingtip vortices a fraction after the pushover began rather than before it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to step clear of the wingtip vortices before the pushover begins, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP maintained positive G through the pushover into the en route descent, holding lateral separation to about 18 ft, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP maintained positive G through the pushover into the en route descent and through every reduced G segment of the route, lateral separation held to about 15 ft with lateral corrections remaining effective at all times and no uncommanded movement toward the leader developing. Stepping clear of the wingtip vortices before the pushover begins, rather than a fraction after, would remove the last trace of drift. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to good low-G discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained positive G through every reduced G segment, lateral separation held to about 8 ft with the position flown clear of the leader's wingtip vortices throughout. The only refinement available was to hold that same G discipline through the steepest pushover of the route. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to very good low-G discipline.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated every reduced G segment, kept the aircraft loaded enough for the flight controls to remain fully effective and stepped the position slightly clear of the leader's wingtip vortices before the pushover, no inboard drift occurring and lateral separation varying by no more than a couple of feet with awareness of the low G limitation above the level expected at this stage of training. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent low-G discipline.

error_modes.label: Leader energy level and power margin left for the wingman

texts.0: SP, as leader, due to extremely low and extremely high power settings flown on the route instead of a constant power setting with smooth changes, did not leave the wingman any margin to adjust for deviations. Power was reduced almost to idle on the descent leg and then pushed to the top of the range in the climb, so the wingman could neither stop the resulting overtake nor regain the position and exceeded the lateral and fore-aft limits. IP intervened to reset the formation energy.
texts.1: SP, as leader, due to power set at the extremes of the range on the climb and descent legs, left the wingman at the outer limits of the tolerances for most of the route, with the observance angle around 50 deg aft in the climb. A workable power setting was established only after IP called for it. No control intervention was needed, but the energy was not managed by SP unprompted.
texts.2: SP, as leader, due to a power reduction taken too far at the first turning point, briefly left the wingman with no room to decelerate and produced a spacing excursion of roughly 20 to 25 ft. SP recognized the effect, restored a mid range power setting appropriate to the altitude block and made the following changes smoothly. No prompting or IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP, as leader, maintained a constant power setting on each leg and made only smooth power changes, keeping the formation at an energy level that left the wingman room to correct both forward and aft. Torque was kept in the working range appropriate to the altitude flown, and the wingman held the fingertip position within the specified deviations throughout. Speed changes at the turning points were made gradually enough to be matched.
texts.4: SP, as leader, held the formation energy so steady that the wingman's power corrections were reduced to small trimming movements for the whole route, including the en route climb and descent. Every speed change was announced and made smoothly from a mid range setting. Energy management for the formation was above the standard expected at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP, as leader, kept the wingman within standards, but flew the climb leg near the upper end of the power range, which left little margin for the wingman to close if the position slipped aft. No tolerance was exceeded and the position was always regained. SP is expected to plan the route energy so that a usable power margin remains on both sides on the next navigation sortie.

texts_at.0: SP, as leader, set the formation power with IP calling the mid-range setting that leaves the wingman a margin to correct, due to this being one of the first formation legs SP has led setting power to leave the wingman a usable margin. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to set more of the power margin independently on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP, as leader, maintained a constant power setting on each leg, holding the wingman's observance angle to about 48 deg, at the edge of the standard, due to the climb leg being flown near the upper end of the power range before it was eased toward mid range. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to plan the climb leg power in mid range from the start, not near the upper end.
texts_at.2: SP, as leader, maintained a constant power setting on each leg, holding the wingman's observance angle to about 40 deg, due to a speed change at one turning point being made a beat quicker than the wingman could comfortably match. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make every speed change at a rate the wingman can comfortably match.
texts_at.3: SP, as leader, maintained a constant power setting on each leg, holding the wingman's observance angle to about 30 deg, due to the power margin on the descent leg being confirmed a fraction after the leg was established rather than before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the power margin before the leg is established, not a fraction after.

texts_above.1: SP, as leader, maintained a constant power setting on each leg, holding the wingman's observance angle to about 48 deg, at the edge of the standard. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP, as leader, maintained a constant power setting on each leg and made only smooth power changes, the wingman's observance angle held to about 40 deg with torque kept in the working range appropriate to the altitude flown. Confirming the power margin before the leg is established, rather than a fraction after, would leave a steadier margin throughout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound formation-energy discipline.
texts_above.3: SP, as leader, maintained a constant power setting on each leg, the wingman's observance angle held to about 30 deg with speed changes at the turning points made gradually enough to be matched. The only refinement available was to hold that same margin through the leader's fastest climb leg. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed formation-energy discipline.
texts_above.4: SP, as leader, held the formation energy so steady that the wingman's power corrections were reduced to small trimming movements for the whole route, including the en route climb and descent, every speed change announced and made smoothly from a mid range setting with energy management for the formation above the standard expected at this stage of training. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional formation-energy discipline.
